analysis.title: US Economics Weekly: Hold then more hikes
key_insights: UBS expects the FOMC to leave the fed funds target range unchanged at the October 27-28 meeting, after the September hike, with Chairman Warsh's message being 'we have more work to do'.
UBS expects a 0.25 pp hike at the December FOMC and now also a 0.25 pp hike at the January FOMC, followed by a prolonged pause to judge whether the three-hike, 75 bp recalibration works.
UBS expects a 10-2 vote in October, with dissents from Beth Hammack and Lorie Logan. One or three dissents would not be a surprise. Kashkari may also dissent.

The October skip reflects the proximity of the midterms and the nature of the inflation problem: 3% inflation not heading to 2% obviously or fast enough, not rising inflation or an overheating economy.

UBS thinks Warsh leaned toward a sequence of three hikes. The strong September CPI likely reinforced the preference for three over two. Williams suggested only one more hike, while Waller's remarks pointed to a possible preference for two more.

UBS expects the October statement to drop the sentence saying they raised rates and to add back 'The Committee will deliver price stability.' Warsh is expected to keep the press conference brief and lean on 'trend not the data point'.

UBS projects 2026 core PCE inflation at 3.2% Q4/Q4, with little progress until 2.9% in the February 2027 data. Headline inflation is projected at 2.1% and core at 2.5% in Q2 2027 as energy base effects are lapped, with core stuck near 2.5% in H2 2027.

UBS tracks Q3 real GDP at 3.6% and real PCE at 3.4% annualized, and Q4 GDP at 1.7% saar. Full-year 2026 growth is 2.5% Q4/Q4 and 2027 is 2.0%. Q3 equipment investment is about 25.2% annualized, with a -2.6 pp net export drag because much of the capital investment is imported.
In 2027 fiscal policy flips from support to a mild headwind as tax refunds shrink, and higher rates weigh more on rate-sensitive sectors. AI investment is expected to stay very robust.

Midterm risk: polling points to more Democratic control of Congress. A Democratic Senate could constrain the administration's Fed Board nominees. UBS expects as many as four governors could depart by early 2028, adding uncertainty about the FOMC's reaction function.

Fiscal deadlines: FY2027 funding and the roughly $500 billion surface transportation bill expire December 11, making a short-term extension plausible. A debt ceiling deal could leave deficits wider than the CBO baseline and raise shutdown risk.

September core CPI rose 0.33% m/m, 0.14 pp above consensus (about 1.6 standard deviations), and the 12-month rate rose to 2.56% from 2.45%. Shelter services contributed 0.08 pp of the surprise, with OER +0.35%, tenant rents +0.25% and lodging +2.04%. Core goods rose the most in about a year.
Headline CPI rose 0.65% m/m and 3.74% y/y, up from 3.40% and versus 2.41% in February before the Iran conflict. Headline is below the 4.25% May peak.
UBS projects September core PCE at +0.35% m/m (3.13% y/y) and headline PCE at +0.52% (3.66% y/y), both up from August (3.01% and 3.42%).

September PPI final demand rose 1.3% m/m and 6.3% y/y, the highest since December 2022. Energy rose 10.8% and core PPI rose 0.5% (5.0% y/y). Import prices rose 1.1% m/m and 8.1% y/y, with fuel imports +34.5% y/y.
Real average hourly earnings fell 0.6% in September, the sixth consecutive monthly decline.
Retail sales control group rose just 0.1% after a 1.2% gain in August. Headline sales rose 0.8% on a 6.4% jump at gas stations.
Industrial production rose 0.7% and manufacturing output rose 0.3% in September (1.1% y/y). High-tech production is up about 17.5% y/y, while manufacturing ex high tech is up 0.7% y/y.

The Empire State index rose to 25.5, the highest since December 2021. The Philadelphia Fed index fell to 20.9, and its ISM-adjusted composite fell to 49.6, which is contractionary. The NY Fed services index fell to -20.7.

Brent front-month is about $105 per barrel, below conflict peaks near $120, with Strait of Hormuz attacks at a wartime high. AAA gasoline is $4.33 per gallon versus a $4.49 peak and $2.93 in February.

Housing is weakening. Mortgage rates are about 7.4-7.5% (MBA contract 7.50%, Freddie Mac 7.40%), purchase applications fell for a sixth straight week to the lowest since February 2025, and existing home sales were 3.99M saar.
Initial claims were 199K, below 200K for a fifth straight week, and continuing claims were 1.710M. NFIB optimism fell to 97.9.

Several Fed officials (Hammack, Waller, Goolsbee) are concerned about AI-buildout demand pressure on inflation. Williams and Bowman see no urgency, and Daly says more adjustments are more likely than not.

Fed officials rejected the idea that higher Treasury yields are doing the Fed's tightening. Williams said 'I don't think they're doing our work for us', and Hammack called bond markets a complement, not a substitute.

The Fed enters its quiet period on October 17 ahead of the October 27-28 meeting. Week-ahead data are mostly housing and sentiment surveys: NAHB, starts and permits, pending home sales, regional surveys, flash PMIs and final Michigan sentiment.

risk_factors: Inflation fails to soften, leading to more hikes than the two UBS expects in December and January.
Persistent AI-buildout demand pressure on prices, especially semiconductors and inputs, which Waller says could last two to three years.
Energy price shocks from the Strait of Hormuz conflict, with Brent around $105.
A Democratic Senate shaping Fed Board composition, raising uncertainty about the FOMC reaction function.
Government shutdown and debt ceiling brinkmanship around the December 11 funding and surface transportation expiry, and wider deficits.
Housing weakness from mortgage rates near 7.5% and bloated builder inventories.
Consumer squeeze: real wages are falling and the Beige Book describes a bifurcated consumer.
Hurricane Isaias shut in roughly 63% of US Gulf of Mexico crude output.
vol_and_positioning: Market pricing of an every-meeting pace of hikes moderated after the October skip was communicated, and the front-end rate move looked more contained, per UBS.
Treasury yields rose and mortgage rates climbed to 7.4-7.5%, but Fed officials say bond markets are not substituting for Fed tightening.
geopolitical: Iran conflict: attacks on commercial vessels around the Strait of Hormuz reached a wartime high of 12 strikes last week, and an oil tanker caught fire east of the Strait.
US-Iran diplomatic talks have stalled, which adds to consumer uncertainty and keeps energy prices elevated.
US midterm elections: a Democratic Congress would raise gridlock and fiscal brinkmanship risk and could limit the administration's Fed nominees.
Tariffs: Williams described tariff effects as mostly in the rearview mirror, though Beige Book contacts still cite tariffs as a risk.

tension_points.bull_case: Hawkish case: Hammack and Logan want three hikes in short order, Waller's remarks suggest a possible preference for two more, and the strong September CPI reinforces a three-hike recalibration (UBS expects Dec and Jan).
tension_points.bear_case: Dovish case: Williams sees one more hike and Bowman and Daly feel no urgency. Musalem notes limited domestic inflationary pressure, and UBS says the problem is slow disinflation, not rising inflation.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Core inflation failing to soften, or the 3.2% core PCE Q4/Q4 projection being revised down in December, which would imply fewer hikes.

theme_stances.key_argument: The FOMC skips October because of the midterms and slow disinflation, then raises 25 bp in December and January.
theme_stances.evidence: we now expect another 0.25 pp increase at the January FOMC meeting

theme_stances.key_argument: A Democratic Senate could constrain nominees and raise uncertainty about the future FOMC reaction function.
theme_stances.evidence: the potential implications of the midterms for monetary policymaking are underappreciated
